sn22.59:1.1: This is the famous “second discourse”, the story of which is told in the Vinaya ([pli-tv-kd1:6.32.1]()). At the conclusion of the Dhammacakkappavattanasutta ([sn56.11]()), when Koṇḍañña became a stream-enterer, the Buddha continued to teach the five ascetics over several days, until all five had realized stream-entry and gone forth officially as Buddhist mendicants. Knowing they were ready, he then taught them about not-self.
sn22.59:2.2: This conditional argument against the “self” is found only here, but it resembles the Buddha’s discussion with Poṭṭhapāda of various kinds of “self” ([dn9:21.4]()).
sn22.59:2.3: Also at [mn35:13.4](). This responds to the “inner controller” (_antaryāmin_) of Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7. Uddālaka, having learned this from the centaur Kabandha in Madra (near modern Islamabad), challenges Yājñavalkya, who explains it as the self who lives in the midst of all things, unknown but knowing, controlling all from within.
